strengths: The paper targets an important and difficult problem: trajectory-controlled panoramic street-view video generation from a single satellite image.
The combination of a tri-plane representation, ray-guided conditioning, and pose-aware epipolar attention is intuitively well matched to the large cross-view gap and sequential setting.
The proposed VIGOR++ dataset is potentially valuable, with approximately 91,500 satellite-sequence pairs spanning ten cities and geographically separated training and test locations.

Experiments cover image quality, semantic and depth similarity, temporal consistency, efficiency, single-image generation, and a downstream localization application; the reported results generally favor the proposed method.
weaknesses: The evaluation omits Sat2Vid, a directly relevant prior method for street-view panoramic video synthesis from a single satellite image that the paper itself cites. Comparisons instead emphasize single-image methods and a generic object-centric view-synthesis model, substantially weakening the main state-of-the-art claim.

Evidence for geometric consistency is inadequate. Predicted-depth and semantic-feature distances do not directly test alignment with satellite geometry, trajectory accuracy, cross-frame reprojection consistency, or recovered 3D structure. The qualitative outputs are plausible but often differ materially from the ground truth layout.

The ablations do not isolate the proposed contributions. There is no controlled removal of the tri-plane, CVHA, ray sampling, or incremental feedback, and the temporal study only compares against full attention. Figure 6 is also internally inconsistent: its row label says 'w/o Temp-Att' while the caption and text describe full cross-attention.

Reproducibility is poor. The paper promises appendix details, but no appendix is included. Essential information is missing, including sequence length and sampling, tri-plane dimensions, ray depth range and number of samples, epipolar-line discretization or tolerance, architectural insertion points, optimization hyperparameters, loss details, and dataset construction specifications.

Metric definitions and reporting are unclear. CLIPSIM is treated as lower-is-better despite being described as similarity; FVD values are unusually small without normalization details; sample counts and evaluation protocols are absent; and no uncertainty, repeated runs, or human evaluation is reported.

VIGOR++ is evaluated only by its creators on one split. The geographic separation and prevention of overlapping satellite regions are insufficiently specified, while Street View panoramas may come from different capture dates and are spatial sequences rather than genuine temporal video. Dataset release and annotation quality are also unclear.

The use and prospective redistribution of Google Maps and Street View imagery raises licensing, privacy, and dataset-governance concerns that receive no discussion. Broader biases and potential misuse in navigation or surveillance applications are likewise unaddressed.

The downstream localization improvement is small and reported without variance or significance testing, so it does not strongly substantiate practical utility. Overall, the promising formulation is not supported by sufficiently rigorous comparisons, ablations, geometric evaluation, or reproducibility details for a top-tier acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses a difficult and practically relevant problem: generating trajectory-controlled street-view panoramas from a single satellite image while maintaining spatial and temporal consistency.
The combination of a tri-plane scene representation, ray-guided feature retrieval, and pose-aware temporal attention is intuitively well motivated.

The proposed VIGOR++ dataset could be a valuable contribution: it reportedly contains more than 90,000 satellite/video pairs across ten cities with geographically separated training and test locations.

The experiments cover image quality, semantic similarity, temporal consistency, computational cost, and a downstream localization application. The reported results consistently favor the proposed method, and the qualitative examples show better realism than the displayed baselines.
weaknesses: The evaluation is not sufficiently convincing for a top-tier acceptance. Only three baselines are evaluated on the main video task, and the paper omits Sat2Vid, despite citing it and its title indicating essentially the same single-satellite-to-panoramic-video problem. Excluding another recent method because its code is unavailable does not resolve the lack of comparison with the most directly related work.

The ablations do not isolate the claimed contributions. There is no decomposition of tri-planes, cross-view hybrid attention, ray sampling, deformable offsets, or incremental scene refinement. The temporal analysis compares only full cross-attention against the complete epipolar variant, so it does not separate the effects of geometry, sparse frame selection, and reduced attention capacity.

There is an internal inconsistency in the temporal ablation: Figure 6 labels the comparison as without temporal attention versus epipolar attention, whereas its caption and surrounding text describe full cross-attention versus epipolar attention. This makes the qualitative evidence difficult to interpret.

Several metrics are inadequately defined or questionable. CLIPSIM is described as a similarity but is marked as lower-is-better and has an unexplained numerical scale. The construction of video clips for FVD, the sample counts, feature normalization, and aggregation procedures are not given. There are no confidence intervals, repeated trials, or statistical tests, including for the small downstream localization improvement from 5.22 to 4.99.

The manuscript claims geometric consistency but primarily evaluates appearance and learned-feature similarity. It provides no direct geometric measurements such as pose-conditioned reprojection error, correspondence accuracy, layout consistency, trajectory drift, or multiview reconstruction quality. The qualitative outputs also visibly differ from the ground truth in structures and scene content, reflecting substantial hallucination.

The method is substantially underspecified. Missing details include tri-plane dimensions and coordinate bounds, ray depth ranges and sample counts, epipolar candidate discretization and tolerance, panorama seam handling, sequence length, pose encoding, optimizer and batch size, and the precise integration points within the diffusion model. The text promises additional details in an appendix, but the submitted manuscript contains no appendix.

The dataset description lacks essential information about sequence-length distributions, sampling intervals, pose accuracy, capture-date discontinuities, annotation quality control, and possible overlap between neighboring satellite crops. It also does not provide a release commitment or address licensing and redistribution restrictions associated with Google Maps and Street View imagery.

The claimed long-range temporal consistency is not tested as a function of trajectory length or displacement. The model attends only to the two preceding frames, yet no drift, loop-consistency, or long-horizon analysis is provided.

The downstream experiment is weak evidence of utility: the aligned and unaligned settings are not defined, the amount of added synthetic data is unspecified, and the comparison does not control for simply training with more examples.

Overall, the core ideas are plausible and the reported numbers are promising, but missing direct baselines, incomplete ablations, metric ambiguities, limited geometric validation, poor reproducibility, and unresolved dataset licensing concerns leave the central claims insufficiently supported. These are meaningful weaknesses rather than minor presentation issues.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and challenging problem: trajectory-controlled generation of panoramic street-view sequences from a single satellite image.
The combination of ray-guided tri-plane conditioning and epipolar-constrained temporal attention is well motivated and incorporates relevant geometric structure into the diffusion model.
VIGOR++ is potentially valuable: it reportedly contains more than 90,000 satellite/trajectory/ground-sequence pairs across ten cities, substantially expanding the available evaluation setting.

The experiments cover video generation, single-image generation, component analysis, efficiency, and a downstream localization application. Reported results are generally favorable across several perceptual, semantic, geometric, and temporal metrics.
The paper is clearly organized, and its qualitative examples suggest improvements in structural continuity and visual fidelity over the displayed baselines.
weaknesses: The evaluation does not yet convincingly establish state of the art. In particular, Sat2Vid, a directly relevant satellite-to-panoramic-video method cited as reference 28, is not compared against or discussed as an omitted baseline. Image-generation baselines are comparatively weak evidence for the central video-generation claim.

Important experimental details are missing, including sequence lengths, trajectory statistics, batch size, optimizer, learning rate, tri-plane dimensions, ray depth range, number of ray samples, epipolar candidate construction, and temporal-attention placement. The paper refers readers to an appendix, but none is present in the manuscript, substantially limiting reproducibility.

The ablation study is incomplete. It compares epipolar attention only with full cross-attention and does not report variants without temporal attention, without ray guidance, without the tri-plane, with alternative spatial representations, or with different temporal neighborhoods. Consequently, the individual contribution of each design choice is not adequately isolated.

Some quantitative reporting is internally inconsistent or insufficiently defined. Table 1 claims the proposed method is best across all dimensions, but it is not best on SegAny under the table's lower-is-better convention. CLIPSIM is also marked lower-is-better despite ordinarily being a similarity measure. Metric scaling, computation protocols, sample counts, and statistical variation are not provided.

VIGOR++ requires much more documentation. The construction process, manual-refinement criteria, trajectory lengths, camera-pose accuracy, capture-time discontinuities, train/test separation, and release plan are unclear. Because nearby Street View panoramas may have been captured at different times, calling the data continuous video or temporally aligned needs stronger justification.

The paper does not address licensing, redistribution, privacy, or terms-of-service considerations associated with collecting and releasing Google Maps and Street View imagery. This is a material concern for the claimed dataset contribution.

The method description leaves technical ambiguities: it is unclear how vertical tri-plane features are learned from a single overhead observation, how previously generated frames are projected back into the tri-plane, and whether generation is joint or autoregressive. The latter mechanism is mentioned but not formalized or evaluated.

The evaluation lacks human preference judgments, failure-case analysis, genuinely long-horizon results, and testing on unseen cities. The small downstream localization improvement is promising but modest and reported without variance or significance testing.

strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem: trajectory-controlled generation of coherent ground-level panoramas from a single satellite image.
The combination of ray-guided triplane conditioning and panoramic epipolar attention is technically plausible and incorporates useful geometric structure into diffusion-based generation.
VIGOR++ could be a valuable benchmark: it substantially expands geographic coverage and provides pose-annotated panoramic sequences for a setting underserved by existing datasets.

The evaluation includes single-view and sequence generation, multiple perceptual and geometric metrics, qualitative comparisons, efficiency measurements, component ablations, and a downstream localization experiment.
Reported results are consistently favorable, especially for multiview metrics, and the qualitative examples generally show better spatial continuity than the displayed baselines.
weaknesses: The empirical comparison omits Sat2Vid, a directly relevant prior work titled "Street-view panoramic video synthesis from a single satellite image." Although cited in the bibliography, it is neither adequately distinguished nor evaluated. This substantially weakens the novelty argument and the evidence for state-of-the-art performance.

Core implementation details are missing despite the reproducibility claim: triplane construction and dimensions, spatial bounds, ray depths and sample count, deformable-offset parameterization, epipolar-point sampling and tolerance, attention locations, conditioning architecture, and several dataset/sequence specifications are not reported. The appendix section advertised as architectural detail instead mainly discusses cross-batch scaling.

The derivation of the panoramic epipolar constraint is technically flawed. The inverse equirectangular projection of a pixel yields a bearing direction, not the 3D point Q as asserted; unknown depths are omitted from Equations 11–14. The final essential-matrix constraint can be valid for bearing vectors, but the provided proof does not establish it correctly. Equation 9 also calls a cross product an outer product.

The evaluation protocol is insufficiently documented. Several metrics, including CLIPSIM, SD, LRCE, and the Pi3-based reconstruction scores, lack precise computation details; the unusual direction and scale of CLIPSIM are unexplained; there are no uncertainty estimates or significance tests; and sequence lengths and FVD sampling details are absent.

There are internal reporting inconsistencies. Table 6 is labeled as a CVUSA experiment, but its proposed-method values exactly match the VIGOR results in Table 2 rather than the CVUSA results. The claim of best performance across all dimensions also overlooks metrics where the method is not best, such as SegAny in Table 1 and some pixel-level measures in Table 2.

The ablations do not cleanly isolate all claimed contributions. There is no full factorial study separating triplanes, cross-view hybrid attention, ray sampling, temporal autoencoder changes, and epipolar attention, and no comparison against standard unconstrained temporal attention with matched capacity beyond the single full-cross-attention variant.

VIGOR++ construction is too vaguely described for assessing bias or leakage: path extraction, manual refinement, geographic splitting, duplicate removal, pose accuracy, sequence-length distribution, and annotation quality control are not quantified.

The dataset relies on Google Maps and Street View, yet the paper does not address redistribution/training rights, privacy handling, or release feasibility. The broader-impact discussion also gives limited attention to geolocation, surveillance, and place-specific misinformation risks.

The downstream localization gain is small and reported from a single training run without uncertainty, stronger augmentation baselines, or controls for simply adding more data, so it provides limited evidence of practical impact.

strengths: The paper targets an important and difficult problem: generating trajectory-controlled, multiview-consistent ground panoramas from a single satellite image.
Combining ray-guided triplane conditioning with panoramic epipolar attention is intuitively well motivated, and the resulting framework addresses both cross-view alignment and temporal consistency.
The proposed VIGOR++ extension could be a useful community resource if its construction, licensing, annotations, and release are adequately validated.

The experiments cover single-view generation, sequence generation, component ablations, efficiency, 3D reconstruction-based evaluation, and a downstream localization task; the reported results are generally favorable.
weaknesses: Novelty is inadequately established against Sat2Vid, whose stated task is panoramic street-view video synthesis from a single satellite image. Despite citing Sat2Vid, the paper neither discusses it substantively nor includes it as a baseline. This omission directly undermines the claimed contribution and empirical positioning.

The derivation of the panoramic epipolar constraint is technically incorrect as written. An inverse equirectangular projection maps a pixel to a bearing direction, not to the 3D point Q as asserted in Eq. 11; depth scale factors are missing throughout the proof. A bearing-vector epipolar constraint may still be valid, but the presented proof does not establish it.

Core implementation details are absent: initialization of the XZ/YZ planes, scene coordinate bounds and scaling, ray-depth range, K and J, candidate-point sampling and tolerance for the epipolar curve, module locations, and sequence inference procedure. Thus, the reproducibility statement is not supported by the manuscript, especially while code and data are only promised.

The sequence evaluation is insufficiently specified. The paper does not state the evaluated trajectory lengths, frame spacing, number of sequences, metric implementations, or aggregation protocol. Training uses only three- and five-frame clips, while qualitative comparisons show five frames, providing little evidence for the claimed continuous or large-scale generation capability or for resistance to long-horizon drift.

Several metrics are poorly defined or potentially misused. In particular, the paper treats CLIPSIM as lower-is-better without explaining its formulation, gives no precise definitions for Palex/Psqueeze or the reported depth metric, and reports no uncertainty or statistical testing. The unusually small FVD values are uninterpretable without implementation and sample-count details.

There are concrete reporting inconsistencies. Table 6 is captioned as a CVUSA experiment, but its Ray-Based Pixel Attention row exactly reproduces the VIGOR results from Table 2. Tables 5 and 6 also reuse the same VIGOR result vector. These errors reduce confidence in the experimental record.

The comparisons do not cleanly isolate the proposed contributions. The main baselines lack equivalent temporal mechanisms, EscherNet is adapted from a materially different setting, and the paper omits directly relevant methods because code is unavailable without offering reported-result comparisons or stronger alternative baselines. The epipolar module is compared mainly against expensive full cross-attention rather than standard video-attention variants.

VIGOR++ is under-documented. The meaning and length distribution of the claimed 90,000 'video pairs,' trajectory-generation and manual-refinement protocols, calibration accuracy, duplicate/overlap control, temporal alignment between satellite and Street View imagery, and geographic split construction are unclear. There is no cross-city or out-of-domain evaluation to substantiate generalization.

The manuscript does not adequately address the licensing, redistribution, privacy, and dataset-bias implications of collecting and promising to release large amounts of Google Maps and Street View data. The generic social-impact section does not resolve these dataset-specific concerns.

The downstream localization improvement is small (5.22 to 4.99 and 5.33 to 5.11) and is reported from a single training run without variance, significance analysis, or controls for simply adding more data.

The paper itself acknowledges that poses less than 8 m apart can yield nearly identical outputs because training views are spaced 15–20 m apart. This is a substantial limitation for navigation, simulation, and 'continuous' scene-generation claims, yet it is not reflected in the main evaluation or conclusions.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and difficult problem: generating trajectory-controlled, multiview-consistent ground panoramas from only one satellite image. This is relevant to simulation, localization, and urban-scene modeling.

SatDreamer360 is a coherent combination of complementary geometric components: triplane scene features and ray-based conditioning address the satellite-to-ground viewpoint gap, while panoramic epipolar attention addresses inter-frame consistency.
VIGOR++ is potentially a valuable contribution. Its reported 90,000-plus satellite/sequence pairs across ten cities substantially expand the data available for this underexplored setting.

The empirical results are broad: the paper evaluates single-view and sequence generation using perceptual, semantic, pixel, temporal, and reconstruction-based metrics. The method leads all reported VIGOR++ metrics and generally improves over prior satellite-to-ground methods on CVUSA and VIGOR.

The appendix contains useful component and efficiency studies. The comparisons of triplane versus BEV, ray-based versus standard attention, sparse versus dense temporal attention, and matched full versus epipolar attention support the architectural choices.

Qualitative examples show a meaningful improvement over the selected baselines in realism and temporal stability, and the localization experiment provides preliminary evidence of downstream utility. weaknesses: The experimental evidence needs more precise reporting. The paper does not define exactly how several metrics—especially DINO, SegAny, Depth, CLIPSIM, 3DPS, and 3DSS—are computed or aggregated, and the unusually small FVD values require explanation. There are no confidence intervals, multiple-run statistics, or significance tests.

The evaluation of an inherently one-to-many task relies heavily on paired reference metrics, which can penalize plausible alternatives. A blinded human evaluation of realism, satellite alignment, and sequence consistency would materially strengthen the central claims.

The sequence baselines are limited. Two principal competitors are fundamentally single-image methods, while EscherNet was designed for a substantially different setting. The paper omits unavailable but highly relevant systems and does not include a strong generic video-diffusion or matched-compute temporal baseline.

The temporal ablation is incomplete. A quantitative no-temporal-attention result is missing, and full global cross-attention is not a clean control for epipolar attention because its computational burden and candidate set differ. A local unrestricted-attention control with the same number of sampled keys would better isolate the value of epipolar geometry.

Claims of continuous, scalable generation are stronger than the evidence. Training sequences contain only three to five frames, quality is not quantitatively evaluated over long trajectories, and attending only to two preceding frames may accumulate drift. The reported failure for camera separations below 8 m also limits applicability to smoothly sampled driving trajectories.

The derivation of Eq. 6 is technically imprecise: inverse equirectangular projection gives a bearing direction rather than the 3D point Q without an associated depth. The final bearing-vector epipolar constraint can be valid, but the proof should explicitly introduce per-view depths and eliminate them.

Reproducibility is presently limited despite the promised release. Important specifications such as triplane resolution and spatial extent, ray depth bounds, sample counts, attention dimensions, baseline training details, evaluation sequence lengths, dataset path statistics, and annotation quality-control procedures are absent or incomplete. Table 6 is also labeled as CVUSA although its ray-attention row duplicates the VIGOR results in Table 5, suggesting a reporting error.

Because VIGOR++ is sourced from Google Maps and Street View, the paper should clarify redistribution rights, release format, privacy handling, and compliance with the source platforms' terms. The current broader-impact discussion does not address these dataset-governance issues.
